newsitem.title: UK: Mowlam says N.Ireland guerrillas must disarm.
newsitem.headline: Mowlam says N.Ireland guerrillas must disarm.

text.p: Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, preparing for talks this week with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, said on Monday that she wanted all guerrilla groups disarmed.
"Decommissioning isn't an arbitrary or unreal issue....We are committed to the total disarmament of all paramilitary organisations," Mo Mowlam told business leaders in Belfast.

But she gave no hint of how she would reconcile wide differences between pro-British unionists and Sinn Fein over when and how guerrillas would surrender arms used in a 28-year war that has killed 3,200.
Mowlam said Northern Ireland's 1.5 million people were "very wary...and quite rightly so" after the July 20 ceasefire by the Irish Republican Army in its war against British rule of the province.
The IRA ended an earlier 17-month truce in February 1996 but called the latest ceasefire to get Sinn Fein invited to peace talks sponsored by the British and Irish governments.

Mowlam said security had been relaxed in response to the IRA truce but said Britain "can't afford to let its guard drop" after a spate of sectarian attacks and an attempted car bombing by an IRA splinter group last week.

"Those who in the past have taken the path of terrorism must play their part in helping to restore normality," Mowlam said in a reference both to Sinn Fein and Protestant parties close to the IRA's pro-British "loyalist" extremist foes.
She was reviewing her first 100 days in office before talks this week with Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams, which are expected to take place on Wednesday.
It will be the first meeting between the two since Mowlam took office. Sinn Fein was barred from ministerial talks with Britain, Ireland and the United States until the IRA truce.
Mowlam said she would decide at the end of the month whether the IRA ceasefire was for real. If so, she would allow Sinn Fein to join peace talks for the first time in September.
"By the end of this month I will make a political judgement, based on all the circumstances in the round, whether or not the IRA ceasefire is genuine," she said.

Mowlam said she would press ahead with the establishment of an international "decommissioning body" to work on the surrender of guerrilla arms while talks on a political settlement to the 28-year Northern Ireland conflict proceed.
But the Ulster Unionist Party, the key voice of the Protestant majority which wants to stay British, says the body must be given powers to force the IRA to surrender weapons.
Sinn Fein's leaders say the IRA will not surrender a single bullet until an overall political settlement is reached.

Mowlam, drawing on groundwork by the previous Conservative British government vanquished in May 1 elections, said Northern Ireland's future was "as a modern player among the regions and nations of Europe".
She made reference to cross-border bodies the British and Irish governments want to set up to foster trade and economic cooperation between the two neighbouring Irelands.

"I see new opportunities for trade and cooperation between Northern Ireland and the Irish republic developing. It makes common sense economically in many areas," she told the "Group of Seven" business leaders of Northern Ireland.

The idea of cross-border bodies was contained in a February 1995 "Framework Document" which proposed new institutions to build not only trade but trust between the overwhelmingly Roman Catholic Irish republic and Protestant-led Northern Ireland.
It will be on the agenda for the talks which resume with an agenda-setting session on September 9 and the first plenary session of what are supposed to be substantive talks on September 15.
